transcript.text: Our Dyson (one of the V ones, purple bits) keeps cutting out after about 5-10 seconds. Not every time - some days it does a whole room fine. It's maybe 5 years old. Already cleaned the filter and checked for blockages. Battery or something else?

Most likely the battery. At 5 years, that's about the age Dyson batteries start to fail, and the intermittent pattern (fine some days, cutting out others) is classic for an ageing battery. As the cells wear, they can't deliver enough power under load. The voltage dips, and the vacuum's protection circuit shuts it off.

## Quick test to confirm

First, check how it cuts out:

• Pulsing (on-off-on-off rapidly) usually means a blockage or airflow problem, not the battery.
• Clean shut-off (just stops, and may restart if you let go and pull the trigger again) points to the battery.

Then try this:

1. Fully charge it.
2. Take off the floor head and run it on the bare wand or body, on normal power (not Max/Boost).
3. Then try it with the floor head on, and on Max.

If it lasts noticeably longer without the head or on low power, but cuts out quickly under heavier load, that's almost certainly a tired battery.

## Other things worth ruling out

• Brush bar: Pull it out and remove any wrapped hair or threads. A clogged roller makes the motor work harder and can trigger cut-outs.
• All filters: Some V models have a second filter at the back of the motor that's easy to miss.
• Cyclone/shroud: The mesh around the inner cyclone can clog with fine dust. A dry brush helps.
• Contacts: Wipe the battery and charger contacts, and check that the battery is seated firmly with no wobble.
• Warning lights: If the battery LEDs flash red, that's a battery or fault indicator.

## If it's the battery

A replacement is usually £40–100 depending on the model and whether you buy genuine Dyson or third-party. Genuine or reputable brands are worth it, since cheap batteries can be poor quality. On most V models it's a DIY job: either two screws or a click-release.

If you check the model number (on the main body, often under the bin or near the battery), I can point you to the right battery and how to swap it.

It's a clean stop, no pulsing. Label says SV11. On Max it nearly always cuts out within a few seconds, and in handheld with no tool it still happens, just less often. No red lights, and the battery isn't swollen or hot. Is it worth the £60+ for a new battery?

## Diagnosis

Yes, that confirms it's the battery. Clean stops, worst on Max, still happening (less often) with no tool attached: that's a worn battery that can't hold its voltage under load. No red lights doesn't rule it out, since the cells can be tired without triggering a fault code.

SV11 is the Dyson V7 (the purple version is usually the V7 Animal).

## Is it worth £60?

Generally yes, if the rest of the vacuum is in decent shape:

• The battery is the main wear part. Motors on these typically outlast several batteries, so a new one should give you a few more good years.
• The alternative costs much more. A comparable new cordless is roughly £150–300+, so £60 is a cheap fix.
• You'll likely get better runtime than you've had in a while, since the decline has probably been gradual.

It's less worth it if the vacuum has other problems (cracked bin, faulty trigger, worn brush head, weak suction even when it runs), or if you were already thinking of upgrading. The V7 is an older model with shorter runtime and no swappable battery, so if that bothers you, it might be the moment to move on.

## Battery options

• Genuine Dyson: usually around £60–70 from Dyson directly. It's the safest choice and comes with a guarantee.
• Third-party: around £25–45. Quality varies a lot. If you go this route, pick a well-reviewed brand from a reputable seller, check for UK/CE safety marking, and avoid suspiciously cheap or "higher capacity" claims. Poor cells can underperform or be a safety risk.

## Swapping it

On the V7 it's a simple DIY job:

1. Empty the bin and make sure the vacuum is switched off.
2. Remove the two screws holding the battery (a small Torx or Phillips screwdriver, depending on the screws).
3. Slide the old battery out downwards and fit the new one.
4. Refit the screws and fully charge before first use.

It takes about 5 minutes. Don't put the old battery in household rubbish. Take it to a battery recycling point (most supermarkets and tips have one).
